Med Tech here. This seems interesting, but we already can detect troponin I in less time than the 60 minutes stated in the article. 1 minute is pretty impressive, but I didn't see any mention of this sensor giving a concentration. Troponin I testing is usually done serially over a several hours to days to chart whether the proteins are decreasing or increasing over time, which helps determine the severity of the MI. I'm sure you are much more familiar with the technical details than I am. Just as a demonstration of that I have to say that the first thing that came into my mind when I read your response was CPK/CK. This tells you how old I am. Like you I hope this new avenue proves useful. It's sort of off topic, but one thing I find "annoying" about the laboratory system in many hospitals is that the time taken up by sample transport and reporting often far outweighs that taken up in the actual 'wet-work'. It would be a happy situation if more tests were able to be done bedside and if lab techs became more of analyzers and transmitters of information in (almost) real time. I recognize that some (most) tests can't be performed outside of the lab, but it would be beneficial for all concerned if they could.

True, specimen transport and reporting results can be a bottleneck. The issue I generally have with the whole "hundreds of tests on one drop of blood" angle is that it doesn't account for reference/reflex testing. Sometimes the results of one test trigger another test, which requires more blood. Now we have to go prick the patient's finger again for another drop of blood. Finger pricks generally hurt more than a needle stick in the arm. If a venipuncture was performed in the first place, more than enough blood is left to run several tests and potentially send the specimen out for more esoteric testing that may not be done in the hospital lab.

That being said, being able to determine if a patient's condition is due to a heart attack within a minute could be useful in an emergency situation.

Ill try to answer some questions :

What did I learn from bugging out? Need to practice bugging out. Planning is not enough. Pack your shit, get to your location and un pack. This will help you realize if you forgot something whether it be major or minor.

What was most time consuming aspect of bugging out? Staying focused and keeping my wife from packing too much. I kept thinking it other stuff I needed to do and pack rather than tackling one thing at a time and finishing it before moving on. My wife kept wanting to pack non essential and easily replaceable things like cases of diapers or bedding. In a different situation those may be necessary, but not this time. I did have one kid to bring, she was napping while we packed that was definitely a time saver. No pets.

What did we bring and how can I decrease time to bug out? We brought a little food and water that was already in the bag. We also packed up everything in the safe which included birth certificates, car titles, mortgage and insurance docs, pictures, external hard drives, some guns and a bit of ammo. I had planned on packing up the safe before, I got some Pelican cases for that stuff. I keep them empty so I can just toss that stuff in there quickly. We also took some clothes for a few days for all of us and some toys for the young one. As far as timing. Practice would help. Also, knowing ahead of time what you want to pack that isn't normally able to be in your bug out bag. Ill be making some lists for myself. Lists would also help from getting distracted.
